newsitem.title: USA: House passes $20 billion energy, water legislation.
newsitem.headline: House passes $20 billion energy, water legislation.

text.p: The House of Representatives Friday passed a $20 billion bill for a variety of next year's programs for cleanup and management of nuclear waste and weapons, and energy and water programs.

The bill, passed 418-7, shifts more resources to water infrastructure projects from energy and nuclear programs, boosting Army Corp of Engineers' water projects by $550 million over the Clinton administration's request and cutting the Energy Department.
The White House said it opposed a number of provisions in the bill, which is $2.6 billion below the administration's request and $573 million below the current level.

Most of the bill -- $15.3 billion -- is for the Energy Department, which a number of Republicans contend is a largely useless bureaucracy that should be eliminated. The bill is $3.2 billion below the White House request, and $474.7 million below current spending.
The bill also specifies several "management reforms" at the Energy Department, which the administration complained was an effort to "micromanage the department."

The bill would provide just $102 million of the White House's $1 billion request for the department to contract out and speed up work to decontaminate the nation's old nuclear weapons production facilities.
The White House said the bill robbed the department of money it needed to privatize more of the costly cleanup in order to meet legally-binding deadlines.
The bill the Senate passed earlier this month provided $343 million to contract more nuclear cleanup work, which the White House said also fell far short of the mark.

The House bill would also transfer a $110 million program from the Energy Department to the Defense Department to restore private industrial sites that were contaminated during the Manhattan Project to develop an atomic bomb.
The White House said that move was unnecessary, and would only increase delays and costs of cleanups.
The bill provides $11 billion for Energy Department defense-related nuclear programs, down $340 million from the current year and down $2.6 billion from the White House request.

It also provides $4.3 billion for civilian energy programs, down $116 million from the current level and down $530 million from the White House request. That includes $285 million for solar and renewable energy programs, up $19 million from this year but $60 million below the White House request.
